rv.q: The original was so perfect that I trudged along to the Theatre Royal Haymarket full of doubts. My pessimism was ill placed. I had a blast.

It’s affectionate fun. There are some good gags – including an early tease of Del’s bar fall – and the sitcom's iconic theme tune works well as a refrain (sung by the cast) for the twinkly cheekiness of this show’s tone.

The finest collection of vintage gags on the London stage should allow the show to make a fair amount of what Del Boy calls “lovely jubbly”. But, as a musical, a few too many of the songs are, to borrow again from the Trotter lingo, plonkers.
The evening is basically a polite nostalgia-fest: certainly not for the era, and perhaps not even for the series itself so much as the feelings it engendered.
It's a well-meaning evening but it needs a generous audience.

The show comes to a head when Del gets a bruising from the villainess Driscoll Brothers after failing to repay the £2,000 loan he acquired to pay for Rodney’s wedding present – part of his deposit for his first flat with new wife Cassandra. But like any episode, the show was never going to end on a downbeat note.

So as a proposition this show makes about as much sense as the mops that tell the time which Del and Rodney sell down Peckham market. And yet, a bit like Del Boy’s made-in-Uzbekistan mobile phone, this show actually works. Set in 1989, the action mostly lingers in the Trotter’s favourite boozer and their council flat.

cn.t: Mixed reception for this musical adaptation, with critics divided on whether it justifies the stage treatment. Strong performances and faithful comic dialogue earn praise, but songs feel shoehorned in and unnecessary to some reviewers.
